abstract.p: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The evolution of North African climate in the Cenozoic is marked by a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic, punctuated by several key transitions and oscillations (1–3). The onset of the arid Sahara occurred around the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene (4, 5), and the persistent drying eventually formed today’s largest desert. A synthesis of available records reveals an overall tendency toward increasing aridity over North Africa during the Cenozoic, superimposed by substantial regional and temporal variability (Fig. 1 and fig. S1). The expansion of the Sahara was accompanied by the retreat of the North African monsoon (NAM), resulting in a narrow rainband to the south of the desert. This climate shift over North Africa has great importance in the Earth system, including modifying the planet’s radiative energy budget (6), seeding Atlantic tropical cyclones (7), supplying dust for ocean productivity (8), driving Late Miocene biotic transitions (9), and influencing the emergence of early hominins in Africa (10).

caption.p: Vertical shading indicates wet or dry conditions, following the interpretations reported in the literature (references numbered above). The results are interpolated onto uniform time intervals for better comparison. A detailed compilation is presented in figs. S1 and S2, including proxy types, sampling regions, and source locations (e.g., figures and text) in each study.

sec.p: Previous studies mainly attribute the aridification of North Africa in the Cenozoic to two factors: changes in global climate and regional paleogeography. After the warm and humid climate of the Early Cenozoic, the global climate began to cool, marked by stepwise shifts such as the Eocene-Oligocene transition (11). Following global trends, the regional climate of North Africa became cooler and drier. Changes in paleogeography also affected North African climate by modulating atmospheric circulations. An influential argument is that the shrinkage of the Tethys Sea was a primary driver of the abrupt onset of the Sahara Desert during the Late Miocene (12, 13). Other proposed paleogeographic factors include the uplift of eastern Africa and the closure of the Indonesian Seaway (14, 15); however, their impacts are considered comparatively minor or limited to shorter timescales.

Here, we demonstrate that the pronounced early Cenozoic aridification of North Africa is primarily driven by the remote influence from the development of the South Asian monsoon (SAM), which experienced enhancement concurrently (Fig. 1 and fig. S2). The antiphase correlation between South Asian and North African hydroclimate is largely driven by the early Cenozoic transition, during which the SAM strengthened substantially in response to the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. The linkage between SAM and NAM in the modern climate is well established as the monsoon-desert mechanism (16, 17): Diabatic heating released from SAM precipitation generates westward-propagating stationary Rossby waves, manifested as a strong upper-tropospheric high-pressure system extending toward North Africa. The monsoon-desert mechanism accounts for the strong anticorrelation between North African precipitation and SAM variability on interannual to decadal timescales in the current climate (18, 19).

Climate variability over North Africa and South Asia, and their potential linkage, has been investigated in modern and paleoclimate on orbital or suborbital timescales (literature synthesis in table S1). Under modern climate forcing (table S1A), North Africa and South Asia exhibit in-phase hydroclimate responses: both becoming wetter under CO2-induced warming [e.g., (20, 21)] and drier under aerosol forcing [e.g., (22, 23)]. Similarly, on orbital and suborbital timescales, most studies report in-phase variability (table S1B). For example, the Green Sahara and an enhanced SAM both occurred in the Middle Holocene under increased Northern Hemisphere summer insolation associated with orbital precession (24–26). This in-phase variability is opposite to the expectation from the monsoon-desert mechanism, implying that the responses to the global or hemispheric forcings potentially mask the effects of monsoon-desert teleconnection over North Africa. Notably, a number of proxy-based studies report antiphase hydroclimate variability between South Asia and regions to its west (e.g., East Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East) on orbital and suborbital timescales [e.g., (27–29); table S1C], with the monsoon-desert mechanism often invoked but not explicitly tested.

These contrasting relationships indicate that the sign and strength of South Asian–North African hydroclimate covariability are not determined by timescale itself, but by the relative magnitudes and spatial structures of the forcings acting on the two regions. Here, we demonstrate that the monsoon-desert mechanism provides a dynamical pathway linking the evolution of the NAM and SAM in response to large paleogeographic forcing (i.e., uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau). As SAM precipitation intensified and migrated poleward during the Cenozoic, a modern monsoon-desert teleconnection gradually emerged, which contributed to North African aridification. This provides a straightforward causal explanation for regional climate change in North Africa and establishes a robust connection between the evolution of the SAM and NAM under tectonic forcing.

sec.title: Coevolution of the SAM and North African climate
sec.p: This study employs two sets of time-slice paleoclimate simulations (Materials and Methods): the L2022 simulations (30) and F2019 simulations (31). Despite notable differences in their numerical models, boundary conditions, and experimental setups, both yield consistent conclusions. We first demonstrate the coevolution of SAM and North African climate throughout the Cenozoic. Figure 2 (A and B) presents the summer climatology from the L2022_default simulations for the preindustrial period (PI, i.e., 0 Ma) and 50 Ma, and results for all time periods are shown in fig. S3. We focus on the summer season (June to August), as most annual rainfall in North Africa occurs during summer. The PI simulation reproduces broad features of the observed summer precipitation climatology well, confirming the model’s suitability for this investigation of changes in continental-scale features [(30); Materials and Methods]. At 50 Ma, the NAM was strong and expansive, with a broad rainbelt extending deep into the continent. Since 50 Ma, a pronounced drying trend is evident, reflected in the expansion of arid zones across the Sahara and an equatorward retreat of the NAM (fig. S3). This long-term aridification is consistent with multiple lines of geological evidence (Fig. 1), including marine and sand deposits (32), stratigraphy (1) and lithology (33, 34), as well as earlier modeling studies [e.g., (13)].

caption.title: Summer (June to August) climatology from L2022_default simulations.
caption.p: The results are at PI (top) and 50 Ma (bottom). (A and B) Precipitation (shading), column water vapor flux (vectors), monsoon regions [green contours; (57)], semiarid (red diagonal hatching), and arid regions [red cross-hatching; (58)]. Red dots mark evaporite records (33, 34). (C and D) One hundred fifty–hectopascal geopotential height anomalies (shading; zonal mean removed), with red contours indicating the 90th percentile, blue contours denoting the 400-hPa diabatic heating (2 K day−1 interval), and black dots indicating areas of strong subsidence (ω > 0.002 Pa/s).

sec.p: Another prominent regional climate change during the Cenozoic is the development of the SAM (35, 36). In the early Cenozoic, the SAM rainfall was relatively weak and confined to the deep tropics (Fig. 2B). As the Indian plate drifted northward, the resulting uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau enhanced monsoonal circulation, enabling the SAM to intensify and expand northward toward the southern slopes of the Himalayas (fig. S3). The Cenozoic development of SAM is well supported by both paleoclimate proxies and simulations [Fig. 1; (31, 37, 38)]. Note that North China is classified within the monsoon region based on its high proportion of summer precipitation; however, its annual precipitation is relatively low, consistent with the North China dry belt during 50 to 25 Ma (39).

The simulated long-term trends of North African aridification and SAM development are consistent across both L2022_default and F2019 (figs. S3 and S5). However, notable differences exist in the pacing of regional climate evolution (fig. S7). Both simulations capture a transient weakening of the SAM between 10 and 5 Ma, in line with proxy records (38), attributed to interhemispheric ice-sheet growth (40) and accompanied by a modest strengthening of the NAM. Arid conditions in North Africa emerge at 35 Ma in L2022_default and 30 Ma in F2019, around the wet-to-dry shift at the Eocene-Oligocene transition in proxies (Fig. 1). The geological record does not indicate a simple monotonic evolution thereafter, but instead shows substantial regional and temporal variability superimposed on the overall tendency toward aridity (Fig. 1 and fig. S1). Nevertheless, both simulations show a strong anticorrelation between the SAM and North African precipitation (Fig. 3A), indicating a persistent dynamical linkage between the two regional climate systems. The antiphase correlation between South Asian and North African hydroclimate is dominated by the early Cenozoic transition, consistent across both proxy records and paleoclimate simulations (Figs. 1 and 3). The coevolution of the SAM and North African climate may arise from the establishment of the monsoon-desert teleconnection as elucidated below.

sec.title: Establishment of the monsoon-desert teleconnection
sec.p: The linkage between the SAM and North African climate via the monsoon-desert teleconnection is evident in the evolution of the upper-tropospheric high-pressure anomaly. In the PI, the rising air of SAM builds an upper-tropospheric anticyclone, the South Asian High (SAH, i.e., the monsoon-desert teleconnection). Under the constraint of Earth’s rotation, the SAH extends westward as a stationary Rossby wave response to the monsoon heating. Because of mass continuity, upper-tropospheric divergence associated with the SAH induces compensating subsidence on its western flank (17, 41), leading to arid conditions over North Africa. In contrast, at 50 Ma, the diabatic heating of SAM is located near the equator (Fig. 2D), where the Coriolis effect is too weak to generate a strong pressure response [(42); an upper-tropospheric high centered over East Asia in Fig. 1D is likely associated with East Asian monsoonal heating]. Across all time periods, the monsoon-desert teleconnection strengthens coherently with the development of the SAM (fig. S4). A similar evolution is seen in F2019 (fig. S6).

The monsoon-desert teleconnection is evidenced by a strong negative correlation between SAM precipitation and North African precipitation (Fig. 3A), and positive correlation between SAM precipitation and subsidence over North Africa (Fig. 3B). Strong correlations among key dynamical and thermodynamical variables in South Asia and North Africa (figs. S7 and S8) further highlight the linkage between SAM development and North African climate via the monsoon-desert teleconnection. Notably, the above mechanism is insensitive to background climate. In a set of fixed CO2 experiments (L2022_fixCO2, Materials and Methods), which exhibit much smaller climate variations, the antiphase coevolution remains evident (fig. S9). Comparison between the L2022_fixCO2 and L2022_default further indicates that, within these simulations, paleogeographic evolution exerts a substantially stronger influence on the SAM–North Africa relationship than the imposed CO2 variations (31).

It is of interest to assess the potential contribution of the Tibetan Plateau, whose elevation increased progressively during the Cenozoic, to the formation of the SAH via elevated heating over the Plateau [e.g., (43, 44)]. We conduct a set of sensitivity experiments in which the main body of the Tibetan Plateau is flattened to 1 km while the Himalayas are retained, for three periods: PI, 10 Ma, and 30 Ma (table S2). Flattening the Plateau leads to a modest weakening of the SAH over the Plateau; however, the large-scale monsoon-desert teleconnection remains largely intact (fig. S10), and precipitation changes are limited outside the Plateau (fig. S11). Consistent with previous studies [e.g., (45, 46)], our results suggest that the uplift of the Tibetan Plateau exerts a secondary influence on the SAH compared to latent heating associated with the SAM, while the uplift of the Himalayas, through its insulation effect, can substantially enhance the SAM and the associated SAH.

sec.title: Linear baroclinic model experiments
sec.p: To directly test the causal influence of SAM diabatic heating on North African climate, we conducted a set of simulations using a linear baroclinic model (LBM; Materials and Methods). The LBM (47) is a simplified dynamical framework with primitive equations linearized around a specified basic state. It is commonly used to investigate atmospheric responses to external forcings and the mechanisms underlying teleconnection patterns (48).

We force the LBM with diabatic heating associated with the SAM extracted from the L2022_default simulations and examine the resulting atmospheric responses. The specified diabatic heating is imposed as a smoothed version (approximated by a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution, fig. S12) of the diagnosed heating, to simplify interpretation. As an example, the LBM results at PI (Fig. 4A) show an upper-tropospheric high-pressure center extending from South Asia to North Africa similar to the SAH (Fig. 2C). The simulated atmospheric responses show the progressive establishment of the monsoon-desert teleconnection, qualitatively similar to the paleoclimate simulations (comparing figs. S13 and S4). At 50 Ma, the high-pressure anomaly driven by SAM heating is very weak and more symmetric across the equator, consistent with the near-equatorial nature of the heating. As the SAM heating intensifies and shifts northward, a modern-like SAH emerges, extends into North Africa, and induces strong subsidence there. These LBM experiments clearly demonstrate that the establishment of the monsoon-desert teleconnection acts as a seesaw transmitting the influence of the SAM to North African climate.

caption.title: LBM-simulated geopotential height anomaly.
caption.p: (A) Same as Fig. 2C but from LBM calculations for the PI case. Regional averaging domains for the SAM, teleconnection region, and North Africa are also indicated. (B) The LBM-simulated geopotential height anomaly at 150 hPa over the teleconnection region, with varying intensity (x axis) and latitude (y axis) of the prescribed heating. The circles represent the L2022 results with number indicating time period.

sec.p: Both the intensification and northward shift of SAM precipitation may contribute to the enhanced monsoon-desert teleconnection. In addition to the increase in SAM precipitation that occurred between 50 Ma and the PI period, the SAM rainfall centroid shifted northward from 10°N to nearly 20°N in L2022_default (fig. S7A; a weaker shift occurred in F2019, fig. S5C). To quantify their relative contributions, we perform sensitivity experiments. Using the LBM simulation at 0 Ma as a reference, we independently vary the strength and the latitude of the prescribed heating. The LBM-simulated responses for different combinations of these perturbed parameters are presented in a matrix, illustrating the parameter dependences of the remote influence of the SAM on North African climate (Fig. 4B). As expected, the high-pressure anomaly (and subsidence over North Africa; fig. S14) strengthens as SAM heating either intensifies or shifts poleward. The effect of a poleward shift of 10°N is roughly equivalent to a 70% increase in heating intensity (i.e., the slope of the color contours in Fig. 4B). The paleoclimate simulation results (circles in Fig. 4B) are qualitatively consistent with the LBM calculations. Specifically, the paleoclimate simulations across all time periods align along a line nearly perpendicular to the color contours, indicating that the poleward shift and intensification of SAM precipitation contribute almost equally to the formation of high pressure and subsidence over Northern Africa.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study demonstrates that the development of the SAM as a major driver of the pronounced early Cenozoic drying of North Africa, based on both paleo-proxies and modeling. The zonal seesaw arises from the monsoon-desert mechanism, which strengthened as SAM precipitation intensified and shifted poleward beyond the deep tropics. LBM experiments establish the causal atmospheric pathway and show that the intensification and poleward displacement of SAM heating make comparable contributions to high pressure and subsidence over North Africa. The particularly strong sensitivity to the latitude of SAM heating reveals an important control on regional circulation that has received limited attention in previous studies. A schematic diagram (Fig. 5) summarizes the key circulation features across different stages of the Cenozoic.

caption.title: Schematic illustration of the monsoon-desert mechanism at different stages of SAM development.
caption.p: (A) Present day, (B) the middle stage (i.e., Miocene), and (C) the early stage (i.e., Eocene). Yellow shading indicates arid regions, while green shading denotes monsoon regions. White clouds highlight regions of climatological intense convection and heavy precipitation. The vertical panels depict the associated upper-tropospheric high-pressure anomaly. Dashed blue arrows mark the large-scale circulation (the upper troposphere is an anticyclone circulation), with arrow size reflecting intensity. The color stars indicate the poleward shift of SAM precipitation.

sec.p: The contrasting relationships between South Asian and North African hydroclimate under different climate states should not be interpreted as an intrinsic dependence on timescale. Rather, their net covariability reflects the relative magnitudes and spatial structures of the forcings acting on the two regions. Global or hemispheric forcings, including CO2, aerosols, orbital insolation, and high-latitude climate changes, can generate coherent hydroclimate responses in North Africa and South Asia (table S1), whereas regional paleogeographic changes that strengthen and poleward-displace SAM heating favor an antiphase response through the monsoon-desert mechanism. During the early Cenozoic transition, SAM forcing was strong enough to contribute substantially to North African drying, whereas at other times, its influence may have been reinforced or masked by competing forcings.

Although SAM development contributed substantially to early Cenozoic North African aridification, other paleogeographic factors may also have played a role. For instance, the shrinkage of the Tethys may enhance the onset of the Sahara Desert (13). However, the timing of Tethys closure remains subject to considerable uncertainty (49). In addition, differences in paleogeographic reconstructions between Zhang et al. (13) and this study may further contribute to discrepancies and uncertainties in the timing of North African aridification. Notably, the retreat of the Tethys has also been suggested to strengthen the SAM (50), which, based on our results, could lead to North African aridification. Future studies should further evaluate the relative contributions of remote (SAM) and local (Tethys) influences on North African climate. Last, it is important to note that the proposed seesaw relationship is presumably unidirectional, as the NAM is unlikely to exert a substantial influence on the SAM.

The geographical configuration that enables a strong SAM-NAM monsoon-desert teleconnection may be unique in Earth’s history, at least on intercontinental scales. Two key conditions must be met to establish such a linkage. First, the driving monsoon must be strong, with its rainfall center located more than 15° off the equator typically requiring prominent geographic features such as large mountains (e.g., the Himalayas for the SAM) or a supercontinent [e.g., the Pangaea monsoon; (51, 52)]. Second, there must be another land monsoon located to the west within the reach of the stationary Rossby wave response (roughly 90° of longitude). A preliminary examination of paleoclimate simulations (30) suggests that over the past 540 Ma, no other monsoon pairs meet these conditions or exhibit a similar linkage. This makes the NAM an outlier among monsoons and helps explain some of its distinctive features. Our findings also have important implications for regional climate evolution, for example, showing how and why subtropical high-pressure centers and ocean gyres evolved in paleoclimates across different timescales.

sec.title: Paleoclimate simulations
sec.p: In this study, two sets of paleoclimate simulations are used. The first set of simulation [(30); short for L2022] is carried out by the authors at Peking University. These simulations use a time-slice approach, covering the period from 50 to 0 Ma (i.e., the Early Eocene to the PI) at 5-million-year intervals. A brief description of the simulation setup is provided here, and full details are available in Li et al. (30). The simulations were conducted using the Community Earth System Model (CESM1.2.2), which includes components for the atmosphere (CAM4), ocean (POP2), land (CLM4), sea ice (CICE4), and river runoff. Dynamic vegetation is simulated using the carbon-nitrogen-dynamic vegetation module in CLM4.

For each geological period, paleogeographic boundary conditions, including continental configuration, topography, and bathymetry, were prescribed using the paleo-digital elevation model developed by Scotese and Wright (53). CO2 concentrations were tuned to match the reconstructed global mean surface temperatures (54) in each simulation. Other atmospheric constituents and orbital parameters were fixed at PI simulation values. Each time-slice simulation includes a low-resolution atmosphere-ocean coupled simulation and high-resolution atmosphere-only simulation. The low-resolution simulations have a horizontal resolution of 3.75° × 3.75°. Each time-slice simulation is run to reach equilibrium (more than 3000 model years). Then, the climatological monthly mean sea surface temperature and sea ice, as well as annual mean vegetation, averaged over the final 100 model years, are used as boundary conditions for the high-resolution simulations. The high-resolution simulations use a horizontal resolution of 0.9° × 1.25° and run for 100 model years. The last 60 model years are used for analysis. The results are similar between the low- and high-resolution simulations, and we focus on the results of the high-resolution simulation (referred to as L2022_default). A set of fixed-CO2 experiments was also conducted to isolate the effect of greenhouse gas forcing. In these simulations, CO2 is fixed at 2800 ppm (10 times the PI level), while all other configurations remain the same as in the experiments described above. This set of simulations is referred to as L2022_fixCO2.

The second set of paleoclimate simulations [(31); short for F2019] was carried out by the author at the University of Bristol. It shares a similar modeling approach to the L2022. However, there are notable differences in the models and simulation settings. The F2019 experiments were performed using the HadCM3 model (HadCM3L v4.5) with a horizontal resolution of 3.75° × 2.5° for atmosphere and 3.75° × 2.5° for ocean, with an interactive vegetation scheme, TRIFFID [see Farnsworth et al. (31) for further details]. The time interval of simulations is uneven following geological stage boundaries; there are 14 simulations from 40 Ma to PI. The paleogeographic boundary conditions were derived from Getech paleogeographic reconstructions produced by the Getech Plc group. The CO2 concentrations were prescribed based on idealized estimations similar to Foster et al. (55). Thus, there is a deviation of approximately 1 K in the time series of global mean surface temperature between L2022_default and F2019. Each simulation was run for 1400 model years and reached quasi-equilibrium.

Both the CESM1.2.2 and HadCM3 models well reproduce key features of modern monsoon precipitation and circulation climatology compared to other similar generation GCMs [(56); figs. S3 to S6]. Evaporite proxies are used here to assess the performance of the paleoclimate simulations. Evaporite formation typically occurs within a net precipitation (precipitation minus evaporation) range of 0 to 300 mm/year. As shown in fig. S15, the evaporite records largely fall within this range in the simulations, corresponding approximately to the margins of arid regions in fig. S3.

sec.title: Linear baroclinic model
sec.p: A simple model, the LBM (47), is used to examine atmospheric remote responses to prescribed heating. The LBM is based on a set of primitive equations linearized around a climatological mean state. Compared to the Gill model (41), it uses spherical coordinates and allows for vertical structure and background winds. In our simulations, the LBM uses a horizontal resolution of T42 and 20 unevenly spaced sigma levels vertically. The basic state is the zonally averaged climatology of boreal summer from the NCEP reanalysis from 1958 to 1997. To force the LBM, we prescribe steady diabatic heating over the SAM region (0 to 40°N, 60 to 90°E). The heating fields are extracted from the paleoclimate simulation at each time period. To reduce noise, we approximate the extracted heating using one (for 50 to 30 Ma) or two (for 20 to 0 Ma) two-dimensional Gaussian-shaped heating distributions (fig. S12). The vertical structure of the heating is also simplified (fig. S12). Each simulation is integrated for 30 days, and the last 10 days are averaged to obtain the equilibrium response.
